title: Sum Array Values
prompt: Given an integer array, calculate the sum of all its elements. Return the total sum.

steps: Start the total at zero.
Visit each element in the array.
Add the current element to the total.
Return the final total.
approach.example: For [2, 4, 3], total changes from 0 to 2, then 6, then 9.

walkthroughSteps: sumArray receives the array by reference.
total begins at zero before processing any values.
The loop adds each nums[i] to total.
The completed total is returned.
commonMistakes: Initializing total with an unrelated array value.
Using i <= nums.size(), which accesses beyond the array.

title: Count Even Numbers
prompt: Given an integer array, count how many elements are even.

steps: Start an even counter at zero.
Check each array element.
Test whether the value is divisible by two.
Increase the counter for every even value.
approach.example: For [3, 8, 6, 5], the counter changes 0 to 1 at 8 and 1 to 2 at 6.

walkthroughSteps: count starts at zero because no values have been checked.
The loop visits every element exactly once.
The modulo operation checks whether nums[i] has remainder zero.
count is returned after all elements are processed.
commonMistakes: Checking nums[i] % 2 == 1 instead of checking for even values.
Incrementing count outside the if statement.

title: Find Minimum Value
prompt: Given a non-empty integer array, find and return its smallest element.

steps: Use the first element as the initial minimum.
Compare each remaining element with the minimum.
Replace the minimum when a smaller value appears.
Return the final minimum.
approach.example: For [7, 3, 9, 2], minVal changes from 7 to 3 and then from 3 to 2.

walkthroughSteps: minVal starts with nums[0] as the current smallest value.
The loop begins at index one because index zero is already stored.
Each smaller nums[i] replaces minVal.
The smallest value remains in minVal when the loop ends.
commonMistakes: Starting minVal at zero when all array values may be positive or negative.
Starting the loop at zero and comparing the first value unnecessarily.

title: Find Maximum Value
prompt: Given a non-empty integer array, find and return its largest element.

steps: Use the first element as the initial maximum.
Inspect each remaining element.
Replace the maximum when a larger value appears.
Return the final maximum.
approach.example: For [4, 9, 2, 7], maxVal changes from 4 to 9 and remains 9 afterward.

walkthroughSteps: maxVal stores the largest value seen so far.
The loop checks every element after the first.
A larger nums[i] replaces maxVal.
The final maxVal is returned.
commonMistakes: Initializing maxVal to zero when negative values are possible.
Using the less-than comparison instead of greater-than.

title: Reverse Array
prompt: Given an integer array, reverse its elements in place and return the modified array.

steps: Set one index at the beginning and one at the end.
Swap the values at both indices.
Move both indices toward the center.
Stop when the indices meet or cross.
approach.example: For [1, 2, 3, 4], swap 1 and 4, then 2 and 3 to produce [4, 3, 2, 1].

walkthroughSteps: left and right identify the two ends of the array.
swap exchanges the values at those positions.
The indices move inward after every swap.
The process ends after all mirrored pairs are exchanged.
commonMistakes: Using left <= right and performing an unnecessary middle swap.
Moving only one index after a swap.

title: Count Positive Values
prompt: Given an integer array, count how many elements are greater than zero.

steps: Initialize a counter to zero.
Visit every array element.
Check whether the current value is positive.
Increase the counter when it is positive.
approach.example: For [-2, 4, 0, 7], the counter increases for 4 and 7, producing 2.

walkthroughSteps: count records the number of positive values found.
The loop examines every element once.
Only values greater than zero satisfy the condition.
The final count is returned.
commonMistakes: Using >= 0 and incorrectly counting zero.
Forgetting to increment count inside the condition.

title: Count Negative Values
prompt: Given an integer array, count how many elements are less than zero.

steps: Start the counter at zero.
Inspect each array element.
Check whether the value is below zero.
Increase the counter for each negative value.
approach.example: For [4, -3, -1, 5], the counter reaches 2 after processing -3 and -1.

walkthroughSteps: count begins at zero.
The loop checks every nums[i].
The condition accepts only values below zero.
count gives the total number of negative elements.
commonMistakes: Using <= 0 and counting zero as negative.
Checking the counter instead of nums[i] in the condition.

title: Calculate Average
prompt: Given an integer array, calculate its average as a double value.

steps: Add all array values into a total.
Convert the total to double.
Divide the total by the number of elements.
Return the calculated average.
approach.example: For [2, 4, 6], the sum is 12 and 12 divided by 3 gives an average of 4.

walkthroughSteps: total accumulates every array value.
The loop finishes with the complete sum.
static_cast<double> prevents integer division.
The sum is divided by nums.size() to obtain the average.
commonMistakes: Returning total / nums.size() as integers.
Dividing inside the loop before the full sum is available.

title: Search Array Value
prompt: Given an integer array and a target value, return true if the target occurs in the array.

steps: Visit each array element from left to right.
Compare the current value with the target.
Return true when a match is found.
Return false if the loop finishes without a match.
approach.example: For [4, 7, 2] and target 7, the comparisons fail at 4 and succeed at 7.

walkthroughSteps: containsValue receives the target to search for.
The loop checks each array position.
A matching nums[i] immediately returns true.
If no match exists, false is returned after the loop.
commonMistakes: Using assignment = instead of comparison ==.
Returning false immediately after the first non-matching element.

title: Reverse String
prompt: Given a string, reverse its characters in place and return the modified string.

steps: Place one index at each end of the string.
Swap the characters at those positions.
Move both indices toward the center.
Stop after all mirrored characters are swapped.
approach.example: For 'code', swap c and e, then o and d, producing 'edoc'.

walkthroughSteps: reverseString stores the input in text.
left and right identify mirrored characters.
swap exchanges the characters while the indices move inward.
The modified text is returned.
commonMistakes: Using left <= right when a strict inward comparison is enough.
Forgetting that text is a local copy and returning the modified string.

title: Count Vowels
prompt: Given a lowercase English string, count how many characters are vowels.

steps: Start a vowel counter at zero.
Inspect each character in the string.
Check whether the character is one of the five vowels.
Increase the counter for every vowel.
approach.example: For 'apple', the vowels a and e increase the counter from 0 to 2.

walkthroughSteps: count records the number of vowels found.
The loop visits every character in text.
The condition checks all five lowercase vowel characters.
The completed count is returned.
commonMistakes: Forgetting one of the five vowel checks.
Comparing text[i] with a string such as 'a' instead of the character 'a'.

title: Check Palindrome
prompt: Given a string, determine whether it reads the same from both ends.

steps: Set indices at both ends of the string.
Compare the characters at both indices.
Return false when a pair differs.
Move inward until the indices meet.
approach.example: For level, l matches l, e matches e, and the middle v needs no comparison, so the result is true.

walkthroughSteps: left and right point to the first and last characters.
Each pair is compared for equality.
A mismatch immediately proves the string is not a palindrome.
If every pair matches, true is returned.
commonMistakes: Comparing adjacent characters instead of mirrored characters.
Moving the indices in the wrong direction after each comparison.

title: Count Digits
prompt: Given a non-negative integer, return the number of digits it contains.

steps: Handle zero as a one-digit number.
Repeatedly divide the number by ten.
Increase the digit counter after each division.
Return the counter.
approach.example: For 583, divide to 58, then 5, then 0, increasing the count from 0 to 3.

walkthroughSteps: The zero case returns one because zero has one digit.
Each division by ten removes the last digit.
count increases once for every removed digit.
The counter equals the original number's digit count.
commonMistakes: Returning zero for input zero.
Using number >= 0 in the while loop, which never terminates after reaching zero.

title: Sum Digits
prompt: Given a non-negative integer, calculate the sum of all its digits.

steps: Start the digit sum at zero.
Take the last digit using modulo ten.
Add that digit to the sum.
Remove the last digit by dividing by ten.
approach.example: For 472, extract 2, then 7, then 4, producing a sum of 13.

walkthroughSteps: total stores the sum of extracted digits.
number % 10 obtains the current last digit.
number /= 10 removes that digit from the working number.
The loop ends when all digits have been processed.
commonMistakes: Using division instead of modulo to extract the last digit.
Forgetting to divide number inside the loop.

title: Check Even Number
prompt: Given an integer, determine whether it is even.

steps: Divide the number by two using modulo.
Check whether the remainder is zero.
Return true for a zero remainder.
Return false otherwise.
approach.example: For 18, 18 % 2 is 0, so the function returns true.

walkthroughSteps: isEven receives the integer to test.
The modulo operator finds the remainder after division by two.
An even number has remainder zero.
The comparison directly produces the boolean result.
commonMistakes: Using number % 2 == 1 without considering the requested even condition.
Using division instead of modulo to test divisibility.

title: Factorial Value
prompt: Given a non-negative integer, calculate its factorial.

steps: Start the result at one.
Multiply the result by each integer from one through the input.
Continue until the input value is reached.
Return the factorial.
approach.example: For 4, result changes from 1 to 1, then 2, then 6, then 24.

walkthroughSteps: result begins at one because it is the multiplicative identity.
The loop starts at two since multiplying by one changes nothing.
Each value is multiplied into result.
The final result is the factorial.
commonMistakes: Starting result at zero, which makes every factorial zero.
Using value < number and skipping the final multiplication.

title: Power Of Two
prompt: Given a positive integer, determine whether it is a power of two.

steps: Reject values below one.
Repeatedly divide even values by two.
Stop when the value becomes odd.
Return true only when the remaining value is one.
approach.example: For 16, the value changes 16 to 8, then 4, then 2, then 1, so the result is true.

walkthroughSteps: Values below one cannot be powers of two.
Every power of two can be repeatedly divided by two without a remainder.
The loop removes factors of two from number.
Only a final value of one indicates a valid power of two.
commonMistakes: Accepting zero as a power of two.
Dividing without checking that number is divisible by two.

title: Greatest Common Divisor
prompt: Given two positive integers, find their greatest common divisor.

steps: Keep the two numbers as the current pair.
Find the remainder of the first by the second.
Replace the pair with the second number and remainder.
Continue until the remainder becomes zero.
approach.example: For 18 and 12, the pairs become (12, 6), then (6, 0), so the GCD is 6.

walkthroughSteps: The loop continues while second contains a nonzero remainder.
remainder stores first modulo second.
The pair shifts so second becomes the new first value.
When second reaches zero, first is the greatest common divisor.
commonMistakes: Updating first before calculating the remainder.
Continuing while first is nonzero instead of checking second.

title: Find Second Largest
prompt: Given an integer array with at least two distinct values, return the second largest distinct value.

steps: Track the largest and second largest values.
Update both when a new largest value appears.
Update only the second largest for values between them.
Return the second largest value.
approach.example: For [8, 3, 6, 9], the largest becomes 8 then 9, while second largest becomes 6.

walkthroughSteps: largest stores the biggest value seen so far.
second stores the best distinct value below largest.
A new largest pushes the previous largest into second.
The final second value is returned.
commonMistakes: Allowing a duplicate of largest to become the second largest.
Updating second before saving the previous largest.

title: Move Zeros Right
prompt: Given an integer array, move all zeros to the end while keeping the relative order of nonzero values.

steps: Track the position where the next nonzero value belongs.
Scan the array from left to right.
Swap each nonzero value into that position.
Leave the remaining positions as zeros.
approach.example: For [0, 4, 0, 2], nonzero values move forward to produce [4, 2, 0, 0].

walkthroughSteps: write marks the next position for a nonzero value.
The loop examines every array element.
Each nonzero value is swapped into the write position.
After all nonzero values are placed, remaining positions contain zeros.
commonMistakes: Incrementing write when a zero is encountered.
Creating a second array when the operation can be done in place.

title: Find Array Index
prompt: Given an integer array and a target value, return the index of its first occurrence. Return -1 if the target is absent.

steps: Scan the array from the first position.
Compare each value with the target.
Return the current index when a match appears.
Return -1 if the scan finishes without a match.
approach.example: For [5, 8, 3, 8] and target 8, the first match occurs at index 1, so the result is 1.

walkthroughSteps: findIndex checks positions from left to right.
The first matching nums[i] immediately determines the answer.
Returning inside the loop prevents later duplicate matches from replacing the first one.
A complete unsuccessful scan returns -1.
commonMistakes: Returning the value nums[i] instead of its index i.
Continuing after the first match and accidentally returning a later occurrence.

title: Copy Array
prompt: Given an integer array, create and return a new array containing the same elements in the same order.

steps: Create an empty result array.
Visit each value in the input array.
Append each value to the result.
Return the completed copy.
approach.example: For [2, 5, 7], values 2, 5, and 7 are appended in order to produce [2, 5, 7].

walkthroughSteps: result starts as an empty vector.
The loop visits every element of nums.
push_back adds each element to the end of result.
The new vector is returned without changing nums.
commonMistakes: Returning nums directly instead of constructing a separate result.
Using the wrong loop bound and skipping the final element.

title: Double Array Values
prompt: Given an integer array, return a new array where every element is multiplied by two.

steps: Create an empty result array.
Visit each input value.
Multiply the current value by two.
Store the doubled value in the result.
approach.example: For [2, 4, 5], the values become 4, 8, and 10, producing [4, 8, 10].

walkthroughSteps: result provides storage for the transformed values.
Each nums[i] is processed exactly once.
Multiplication by two creates the required transformed value.
The new vector preserves the original order.
commonMistakes: Changing nums when the function should create a new array.
Multiplying the entire result by two instead of each element.

title: Replace Negatives
prompt: Given an integer array, replace every negative value with zero and return the modified array.

steps: Scan every array element.
Check whether the current value is negative.
Replace negative values with zero.
Leave non-negative values unchanged.

The condition identifies values below zero.
A negative nums[i] is overwritten with zero.
All non-negative values remain unchanged.
commonMistakes: Using <= 0 and replacing existing zeros unnecessarily.
Writing nums[i] == 0 instead of assigning nums[i] = 0.

title: Count Target Values
prompt: Given an integer array and a target value, count how many times the target appears.

steps: Initialize an occurrence counter.
Scan every element in the array.
Compare each element with the target.
Increase the counter for every match.
approach.example: For [3, 2, 3, 4, 3] with target 3, the counter reaches 3 after finding the three matching values.

Every array position is checked.
Each equality with target represents one occurrence.
The accumulated count is returned.
commonMistakes: Returning after the first match instead of counting all matches.
Comparing target with the array size instead of nums[i].

title: Sum Odd Values
prompt: Given an integer array, calculate the sum of all odd elements.

steps: Start the sum at zero.
Visit each array element.
Check whether the value is odd.
Add every odd value to the sum.

title: Product Array Values
prompt: Given an integer array, calculate the product of all its elements.

title: Find First Even
prompt: Given an integer array, return the first even value. Return -1 if no even value exists.

steps: Scan the array from left to right.
Test each value for evenness.
Return the first value with remainder zero.

title: Compare Array Sums
prompt: Given two integer arrays, return the larger of their two element sums.

steps: Calculate the sum of the first array.
Calculate the sum of the second array.
Compare the two totals.
Return the larger total.

secondSum independently accumulates values from second.
Both totals are complete after their respective loops.

Comparing individual elements instead of the final sums.

title: Count Uppercase
prompt: Given a string, count how many characters are uppercase English letters.

title: Number Sign
prompt: Given an integer, return 1 for positive, -1 for negative, and 0 when the number is zero.
